h1: Flaked grains compared: oats, barley, rye and wheat in the mash
title: Flaked Oats, Barley, Rye and Wheat | Craft Beer School
desc: How flaked oats, barley, rye and wheat change body, foam and haze, how much to use in the mash and what to watch for on brew day.
teaser: A handful of flakes can turn a thin pale ale silky or give a stout its creamy head. Here is which flake does what.
standfirst: Flaked grains are one of the cheapest ways to change a beer's body and foam. Each one behaves differently in the mash and in the glass, so picking the right flake and the right amount matters more than most recipes admit.
sections:
Flaked grains are unmalted cereals that have been steamed and rolled flat. The steaming gelatinises the starch, which means it is already cooked and ready for the mash enzymes to convert. You do not need a separate cereal cooker, as you would for raw maize grits or rice.

Because they are unmalted, flakes bring no enzymes of their own. They rely on the diastatic power of your base malt. With a normal pale or pilsner base, flakes up to about 20 to 30% of the grist convert without trouble. Above that, check the enzyme capacity of your malt.

Flakes go straight into the mash with the crushed malt. Do not mill them, since they are already flat and milling turns them to flour that can gum up the lauter.

Oats are rich in beta-glucans and contain some oil and protein. In beer they give a silky, smooth, almost creamy mouthfeel and add haze. That is why they are central to oatmeal stout and to many hazy IPAs.

Typical use is 5 to 15% in a stout or pale ale and up to 20 to 30% in a hazy IPA. The higher end makes the mash sticky, so add rice hulls at around 2 to 5% of the grist to keep the bed open. Our guide to oats in beer goes further.

In India, plain rolled oats from the supermarket are steamed and flaked in the same way and work in homebrew. Check the pack: avoid instant or flavoured oats with added sugar, salt or milk solids.

Flaked barley brings protein and beta-glucan, which build foam and a fuller body. It gives a slightly grainy, dry flavour.

Its classic home is the Irish dry stout, where around 10% flaked barley supports a dense, long-lasting head against the dry roast finish. It also helps head retention in bitters and lighter ales at 5 to 10%. Too much gives haze and a raw grain taste.

Rye adds a peppery, spicy, slightly earthy flavour and a fuller, oily mouthfeel. Flaked rye gives a gentler rye character than rye malt.

Rye is high in gummy compounds, so it is the stickiest flake in the mash. At 10 to 15% you will notice slower run-off. Rice hulls help, as does a short rest at around 40 to 45 °C if your system allows step mashing. Use it in rye pale ales, rye IPAs and some saisons.
Flaked wheat: foam and a soft haze

Wheat is high in protein and low in husk. Flaked wheat gives a soft, slightly bready body, strong foam and a stable haze. It is the traditional unmalted wheat in a Belgian witbier, often at 30 to 50% of the grist alongside pilsner malt.

In a pale ale or lager, 3 to 8% flaked wheat improves head retention without making the beer cloudy enough to notice. Our guide to beer foam science explains why protein helps.

• Want silkier body and haze: oats.
  • Want a dense, lasting head and dry finish: barley.
  • Want spice and a fuller, oily feel: rye.
  • Want foam and a soft, bready haze: wheat.

You can combine them. A hazy IPA might use oats for body and wheat for foam. A dry stout might pair flaked barley with a little oat for smoothness.

One Indian option many homebrewers overlook is poha, flattened rice. It is steamed and rolled much like other flakes and can lighten the body of a lager, though it adds fermentable sugar rather than body or foam. Use plain thick poha and treat it as you would any rice adjunct.

The best way to learn the flakes is to brew one base beer and split it. Make a 20 litre pale ale with 90% pale malt and 10% of one flake, then repeat with each of the other three. Keep the hops, yeast and mash temperature identical. Taste the four side by side when they are ready.

You will notice the differences in mouthfeel more than in aroma. The oat beer coats the tongue, the barley beer holds a firmer head, the rye beer has a slight peppery bite and the wheat beer feels soft with a lasting foam. Once you have tasted them together, recipe notes like 10% flaked barley stop being abstract.

Stir the mash well, since flakes tend to clump and float. Recirculate a little longer before running off, because protein-rich flakes can cloud the first runnings. Expect a lower extract efficiency than from malt. Plan your gravity accordingly. Track it in your brew log, so you learn what your system actually gets from each flake.
faqs: Do flaked grains need to be mashed?
Yes. They need enzymes from base malt to convert their starch. They are pre-gelatinised, so they can go straight into the mash without a cereal cook.
How much flaked oats should I use?
Around 5 to 15% for body in a stout or pale ale, up to 20 to 30% in a hazy IPA with rice hulls to help the lauter.
Can I use supermarket rolled oats?
Plain rolled oats work. Avoid instant or flavoured oats with added sugar, salt or milk solids.
Why is my mash stuck with rye?
Rye is high in gummy compounds. Add rice hulls, keep rye to a moderate share and recirculate slowly.
